rv.q: It’s a richly thoughtful piece, and with it Steiner joins an august list of playwrights
Yet a vital sense of disturbance is almost entirely absent.
‘Lemons Lemons Lemons Lemons Lemons’ is still good after its richly deserved West End glow-up, it’s just that it’s gone a little sour.
I found the evening twee, contrived and implausible - a bit of a lemon, in fact.
The staging is pseudish, the plotting episodic and the script bland for a play about the value of language.
It’s a compelling argument for art as a means of expression – for when words just aren’t enough.
This is good, clean fun — neither terribly profound nor terribly clever, but entertaining nonetheless.
Lemons forces the audience to contemplate the horror of a wordless life, but outstays its welcome.
For all Turner and Coleman’s energy, you never quite get to know this couple, so the play feels less profound and less moving than it should.
In the end, the rather cool perfection of the production works less well than fringe versions of the play, whose intimacy gives it a more powerful sense of life.
Overall, sadly, it is a bit of a lemon.
The thing is harmless enough but impossible to get fired up about.
Josie Rourke's production is beautifully balanced and predicated on the deep connection between two people that is, by definition, unspoken.
Coleman and Turner’s ability to flick between the two is impressive and peels away the layers of a troubled relationship in fascinating fashion.
Steiner’s debut is flawed, but gloriously ambitious.

cn.t: Critics find Steiner's dystopian romance an intriguing premise that works better as a relationship study than political satire, with mixed views on whether its concept sustains a full production despite strong star performances.
